thread.title: Be the chicken - NewsBreak

author: Staff Writer
title: Be the chicken - NewsBreak
text: As a fishing guide, I have the absolute pleasure of taking people out from all over this big blue marble, and a few who I’m pretty sure aren’t from this planet. The majority of these folks get to fish only a few days out of the year — which is unfortunate, because you can tell how much they love the water when they’re out there soaking up the experience. Because most people don’t have the luxury of fishing whenever they want, their skill levels can be a bit on the rusty side. A big part of my job is to make fishing easy and fun for them, so they can enjoy their well-deserved break from the real world in my reel world. One of the best techniques I use for the not-so-professional angler on my boat is a multi-hook rig I call a porgy rig. This rig is used worldwide and has many names associated with it: Chicken rig, up-down rig, high-low rig, cheater rig and the keep-your-wife-happy rig, just to name a few. I use the term porgy rig because porgies are one of my favorite fish to eat, and because I learned to use this rig on the headboat Miss Cortez back it the late ‘70s while I was learning to catch porgies (along with beeliners, lanes, mangs and triggers also — all great eating fish, if you didn’t know already). So, what’s a porgy rig? Well, the basic porgy rig we use in our neck of the woods is a two-hook rig with a weight attached to the leader beneath the hooks. The hooks are attached to dropper loops tied into the leader at varying depths on the line. It’s a little like a sabiki rig, except with fewer hooks and made for catching bigger fish. You can have as many hooks attached to this rig as you like, but from my experience any more than three hooks and you’re just looking for trouble. Remember, the more hooks there are, the better chance you have of hooking yourself — ouch. I personally tie only two hooks to my rigs, with the first one positioned about 6 inches above the weight and the second one about 6 inches above that. Where you position the hooks is up to you, but I have found that the hooks closest to the bottom seem to catch the most fish. The porgy rig is perfect for any kind of bottom fishing our beautiful piece of the Gulf has to offer. For porgies, beeliners, triggerfish, grunts or snapper, I use a 30-pound fluorocarbon leader attached to 15-pound braid on a medium spinning outfit. This setup is just about perfect for any of the nearshore reefs and ledges out to about 50 feet of water. If grouper digging is your thing, just beef up your rod and reel and go to 65-pound braid and 60-pound leader. If anyone ever tells you that you can’t catch grouper on a porgy rig, you can tell them I said they’re crazy. I have not dropped anything other then a porgy rig for grouper in probably 40 years, and I have some monster grouper and snapper to my name. For nearshore waters I recommend using 3/0 circle hooks; for the bigger grouper and snapper offshore, I like 5/0 circle hooks. Inline circle hooks are required by law for the taking of all reef species. One of the best things about porgy rigs is how easy they are to use — if you just reel, reel, reel when you feel the bite instead of trying to set the hook, you’ll catch all the fish you want. Another advantage of circle hooks is that the fish have a very hard time spitting them out once they’re set. With a porgy rig, there is no trying to feel the bite. When a fish takes the bait, you will feel it instantly. I teach people to use this rig all the time because it’s easy to learn, fun to use and it catches fish. So, the next time you’re out in the Gulf with your better half, don’t be chicken to let them drop down a porgy rig a few times. I’ll bet it will make her happy!
